content: Male circumcision is a surgical procedure involving the removal of all or part of the foreskin of the penis. It is performed for various reasons, including religious rituals, medical purposes, or traditional practices, such as initiation into manhood. Since the 1980s, more than 30 observational studies have suggested that male circumcision may provide a protective effect against the acquisition of HIV in heterosexual men. In 2002, three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were initiated in Africa to evaluate the efficacy of male circumcision in preventing HIV acquisition in men. This review examines the findings of these trials, focusing on the effectiveness and safety of male circumcision in reducing HIV transmission among heterosexual men. The objective of this review was to assess the evidence for the protective effect of male circumcision in preventing the acquisition of HIV-1 and HIV-2 through heterosexual intercourse. To achieve this, a comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify all relevant studies, regardless of language or publication status. In June 2007, databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL were searched, along with electronic conference databases like NLM Gateway and AIDSearch. Clinical trial registries, including ClinicalTrials.gov and Current Controlled Trials, were also reviewed. Researchers and relevant organizations were contacted, and reference lists of included studies were examined. The selection criteria for this review included randomized controlled trials comparing male circumcision to no circumcision in HIV-negative heterosexual men, with HIV incidence as the primary outcome. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated methodological quality. A third reviewer resolved any discrepancies. The data were deemed clinically homogeneous, allowing for meta-analyses and sensitivity analyses to be conducted. Three large RCTs were conducted between 2002 and 2006 in South Africa (N = 3,274), Uganda (N = 4,996), and Kenya (N = 2,784). All three trials were terminated early due to significant findings during interim analyses. A meta-analysis was performed, combining survival estimates from all three trials at 12 months and at 21 or 24 months using a random-effects model. At 12 months, the incidence risk ratio (IRR) was 0.50 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.34 to 0.72), indicating a 50% relative reduction in the risk of acquiring HIV following circumcision. At 21 or 24 months, the IRR was 0.46 (95% CI: 0.34 to 0.62), corresponding to a 54% relative risk reduction. There was minimal statistical heterogeneity between the trial results, with I² values of 0% in both analyses. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the calculated IRRs. Meta-analyses of reported IRRs, per-protocol IRRs, and full intention-to-treat analyses consistently demonstrated significant protective effects of circumcision. Secondary outcomes related to sexual behavior were also analyzed for the Kenyan and Ugandan trials, revealing no significant differences between circumcised and uncircumcised men. However, in the South African trial, circumcised men reported a statistically significant higher mean number of sexual contacts at the 12-month visit (5.9 versus 5.0; p < 0.001) and at the 21-month visit (7.5 versus 6.4; p = 0.0015). No other significant differences in sexual behavior were observed. The incidence of adverse events following the surgical circumcision procedure was low across all three trials. While the reporting of methodological quality varied, the potential for significant biases affecting the results was judged to be low to moderate. This assessment was based on the large sample sizes, the balance of confounding variables across randomized groups at baseline, and the use of acceptable statistical early stopping rules. In conclusion, there is strong evidence that medical male circumcision reduces the risk of HIV acquisition in heterosexual men by 38% to 66% over a 24-month period. The procedure is associated with a very low incidence of adverse events, indicating that it is safe when performed under appropriate conditions. These findings support the inclusion of male circumcision in current HIV prevention guidelines. However, further research is needed to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness of implementing male circumcision as a public health intervention in different local contexts.
